lessons.title: Phantom image QC: federal purpose and timing
lessons.summary: Screen-film facilities must run an FDA-approved phantom image quality test at least weekly; a failed phantom test blocks further exams on the failed component until corrected.

explanation.heading: Weekly phantom rule (screen-film text)
explanation.body: § 900.12(e)(2) requires facilities with screen-film systems to perform an image quality evaluation using an FDA-approved phantom at least weekly, with optical-density and accreditation-body score limits stated in that paragraph.

explanation.heading: Digital path is not a free pass
explanation.body: For FFDM/DBT, § 900.12(e)(6) points to manufacturer-recommended QA (or FDA Alternative Standard #24 using the ACR DMQC Manual). Phantom procedure worksheets and pass/fail scoring tables stay in those manuals—link-only here.

explanation.heading: Failed phantom → stop clinical use
explanation.body: Under § 900.12(e)(8), phantom image testing is on the before-further-examinations corrective-action list. Document the problem, fix it, and keep proof.

lessons.example: A technologist's weekly phantom score is outside the facility's action limits: the unit is not used for patients until the source is fixed and retested.

misconception.belief: Phantom QC can wait until the physicist annual survey.
misconception.correction: Federal screen-film text sets a weekly floor; digital follows manufacturer or Alt Standard #24 frequencies—not 'annual only.'

variants.simpler: Screen-film facilities must run an FDA-approved phantom image quality test at least weekly; a failed phantom test blocks further exams on the failed component until corrected.
variants.example: A technologist's weekly phantom score is outside the facility's action limits: the unit is not used for patients until the source is fixed and retested.
variants.deeper: Under § 900.12(e)(8), phantom image testing is on the before-further-examinations corrective-action list. Document the problem, fix it, and keep proof.

lessons.title: Digital QC path and why detector calibration exists
lessons.summary: Digital mammography QA must track the manufacturer program—or FDA Alternative Standard #24 (ACR DMQC)—and still obey the 3.0 mGy phantom dose ceiling. Detector calibration is a manufacturer/manual procedure, not a freestyle technologist invention.

explanation.heading: Default digital rule
explanation.body: § 900.12(e)(6) says nonscreen-film QA shall be substantially the same as the image-receptor manufacturer's recommended program, except dose still cannot exceed the screen-film phantom ceiling of 3.0 mGy.

explanation.heading: Alternative Standard #24
explanation.body: FDA approved using the ACR Digital Mammography QC Manual (+ DBT Supplement) with the ACR Digital Mammography Phantom as an alternative to manufacturer QC for FFDM/DBT. That is a regulatory permission, not a license to photocopy ACR worksheets into Mammo.

explanation.heading: Detector calibration purpose (principle level)
explanation.body: Manufacturer (or ACR DMQC) programs include detector calibration so the receptor's response stays within the vendor's expected range. Exact steps, tools, and pass/fail numbers are manual-specific—link-only.

lessons.example: A site electing Alt Standard #24 follows ACR DMQC technologist tests for its FFDM unit instead of the OEM binder, but still must keep phantom dose ≤ 3.0 mGy.

misconception.belief: Any technologist can invent detector calibration steps if images look fine.
misconception.correction: Calibration procedures come from the manufacturer or the FDA-accepted ACR DMQC alternative—not ad hoc judgment.

variants.simpler: Digital mammography QA must track the manufacturer program—or FDA Alternative Standard #24 (ACR DMQC)—and still obey the 3.0 mGy phantom dose ceiling. Detector calibration is a manufacturer/manual procedure, not a freestyle technologist invention.
variants.example: A site electing Alt Standard #24 follows ACR DMQC technologist tests for its FFDM unit instead of the OEM binder, but still must keep phantom dose ≤ 3.0 mGy.
variants.deeper: Manufacturer (or ACR DMQC) programs include detector calibration so the receptor's response stays within the vendor's expected range. Exact steps, tools, and pass/fail numbers are manual-specific—link-only.

lessons.title: Compression QC: federal force limits vs manual thickness tests
lessons.summary: Federal rules set semiannual compression force performance limits for screen-film systems and put compression-device failures on the before-further-exams list. Thickness-indicator procedures are ACR/manufacturer detail (link-only).

explanation.heading: Force performance (federal numbers)
explanation.body: § 900.12(e)(4)(iii): at least 111 N (25 lb) available; initial power-drive maximum between 111 N and 200 N (25–45 lb) after Oct 28, 2002. Screen-film text places this among semiannual tests.

explanation.heading: Corrective timing
explanation.body: Compression device performance is listed in § 900.12(e)(8)(ii)(A)—failures must be corrected before further examinations on the failed component.

explanation.heading: Thickness indicator stays in the manual
explanation.body: Compression thickness indicator accuracy checks, tools, and tolerances are specified in the ACR DMQC Manual or manufacturer QC. This module links those manuals and does not reprint their procedures.

lessons.example: Power drive maxes out above 45 lb on the gauge: stop clinical use until compression is serviced and retested.

misconception.belief: Federal law publishes the ACR thickness-indicator pass/fail table.
misconception.correction: Federal text states force limits; thickness-indicator criteria remain in copyrighted manuals.

lessons.title: Visual / cleanliness checks: federal floor, manual checklist
lessons.summary: MQSA requires documented cleanliness protocols for darkroom, screens, and view boxes. Modern digital 'visual checklist' line items live in ACR/manufacturer QC manuals and are cited link-only.

explanation.heading: Federal cleanliness duty
explanation.body: § 900.12(e)(11) requires adequate protocols for darkroom, screen, and view box cleanliness and documentation that cleaning happens at the protocol frequencies.

explanation.heading: Viewing aids
explanation.body: § 900.12(b)(14)–(15) require hot-lights and film masking devices for interpreting physicians—viewing conditions are part of the quality system, not optional furniture.

explanation.heading: Digital visual checklist contents
explanation.body: Which switches, paddles, cables, and room items appear on today's technologist visual checklist—and what finding fails—are ACR DMQC / manufacturer worksheet content. Link-only; do not memorize invented lists from this app.

lessons.example: Inspector asks for the facility's cleanliness protocol and cleaning logs—not only a verbal claim that the room 'looks fine.'

misconception.belief: If the room looks clean, no written cleanliness protocol is needed.
misconception.correction: Federal text requires written protocols and documented frequencies for the listed cleaning items.

lessons.title: Repeat/reject analysis: the federal 2% change trigger
lessons.summary: Screen-film MQSA text requires investigating when the total repeat/reject rate changes by more than 2.0% of films analyzed, then recording corrective actions and assessing whether they worked.

explanation.heading: The 2% change rule
explanation.body: § 900.12(e)(3)(ii): if the total repeat or reject rate changes from the previously determined rate by more than 2.0 percent of the total films included in the analysis, determine the reason(s).

explanation.heading: Close the loop
explanation.body: Corrective actions must be recorded and their results assessed—not only discussed. That effectiveness loop matches the broader MQSA corrective-action culture.

explanation.heading: Digital worksheets
explanation.body: How digital sites compute categories and thresholds day-to-day follows manufacturer or ACR DMQC forms. Federal text still teaches the investigation-and-assessment principle; detailed category taxonomies stay link-only.

lessons.example: Repeat rate jumps from 2% to 5% of films in the analysis window: the facility investigates causes (positioning, motion, exposure), documents fixes, and checks whether the rate returns.

misconception.belief: Repeat analysis is optional if EQUIP periodic review is done.
misconception.correction: Repeat/reject analysis is a separate QC activity; EQUIP FAQ materials note it is not a substitute for periodic clinical image review.

variants.simpler: Screen-film MQSA text requires investigating when the total repeat/reject rate changes by more than 2.0% of films analyzed, then recording corrective actions and assessing whether they worked.
variants.example: Repeat rate jumps from 2% to 5% of films in the analysis window: the facility investigates causes (positioning, motion, exposure), documents fixes, and checks whether the rate returns.
variants.deeper: Pair this with EQUIP lessons: clinical image sample review and repeat analysis answer different questions.

lessons.title: Monitors and viewing: federal viewing aids plus digital QC path
lessons.summary: Federal rules still require hot-lights and masking for interpretation and cleanliness protocols for view boxes. Acquisition/interpretation monitor calibration patterns (SMPTE/TG18 and similar) are manufacturer or ACR DMQC procedures—link-only.

explanation.heading: Hardcopy-era viewing duties that still teach the principle
explanation.body: Hot-lights brighter than the view box and masking devices that crop illumination to the exposed image are required under § 900.12(b)(14)–(15). Cleanliness protocols cover view boxes under (e)(11).

explanation.heading: Digital displays follow the digital QC path
explanation.body: Monitor cleanliness, calibration, and test-pattern QC for acquisition and interpretation workstations are part of manufacturer QA or ACR DMQC under Alt Standard #24—not free inventing of luminance numbers.

explanation.heading: Action limits still matter
explanation.body: § 900.12(e)(8)(i) says nonscreen-film results are compared to manufacturer-recommended action limits. Failed digital QC that falls under (e)(6) is on the before-further-exams list.

lessons.example: An interpretation workstation fails its facility's monitor QC pattern check: follow the site's manufacturer/ACR procedure and corrective timing before using that display for final reads.

misconception.belief: Any bright office monitor is fine for final mammography interpretation without QC.
misconception.correction: Digital interpretation displays are governed by the facility's accepted digital QA program and action limits.

lessons.title: Major physicist tests: federal purposes (not cookbook steps)
lessons.summary: The annual survey must cover annual equipment tests and weekly phantom performance. Federal screen-film text states purposes and numeric limits for collimation/alignment, resolution, AEC, HVL, dose, and artifacts; digital-specific SNR/CNR/MTF details remain ACR/manufacturer link-only.

explanation.heading: What the survey must cover
explanation.body: § 900.12(e)(9) requires the physicist survey to include annual tests in (e)(5)/(e)(6) and the weekly phantom image quality test in (e)(2), plus review of facility QC results and corrective actions.

explanation.heading: Collimation / alignment purpose
explanation.body: (e)(5)(vii) checks x-ray field vs receptor edges (≤2% SID beyond edges) and that the paddle chest-wall edge does not cast a visible shadow.

explanation.heading: Resolution, AEC, HVL, dose, artifacts
explanation.body: Resolution/focal-spot condition, AEC performance and reproducibility, HVL, ≤3.0 mGy phantom dose, and system artifact evaluation are annual federal purposes. SNR/CNR/MTF cookbook values for digital units stay in ACR/manufacturer manuals.

lessons.example: Physicist report flags collimation exceeding 2% SID beyond a receptor edge: facility corrects before relying on that geometry, consistent with survey recommendations and applicable corrective timing.

misconception.belief: Technologists perform annual HVL and dose tests instead of the medical physicist.
misconception.correction: Survey tests are performed by a medical physicist or someone under a physicist's direct supervision.

lessons.title: True laterals (ML/LM): diagnostic purpose, criteria still thin
lessons.summary: Diagnostic mammography uses individualized additional angles beyond routine screening views. A 90° ML is commonly obtained when triangulation/localization is needed (link-only clinical literature). Detailed ML vs LM selection recipes remain ACR-criteria territory.

explanation.heading: Why extra angles exist
explanation.body: NCI: diagnostic mammography uses more angles than screening. MQSA audit language: diagnostic exams use individualized views for symptoms or abnormal screening findings.

explanation.heading: ML in the localization pathway
explanation.body: Link-only clinical DBT implementation literature notes a 90° mediolateral (ML) view is frequently obtained for diagnostic triangulation. That supports purpose-level study; it is not a full ARRT checklist of ML/LM evaluation criteria.

explanation.heading: What stays blocked / needs source
explanation.body: Step-by-step ML vs LM choice rules and 'side of interest nearest the receptor' evaluation criteria are taught in copyrighted ACR clinical image quality / positioning references. Until those are maintainer link-only source-checked, do not treat invented criteria as verified.

lessons.example: A finding seen on CC and MLO needs a true lateral to refine superior-inferior localization before biopsy planning—your site's protocol may call for ML.

misconception.belief: Screening always includes ML and LM on every patient.
misconception.correction: Screening uses routine views; laterals are individualized diagnostic/problem-solving views unless a protocol says otherwise.

variants.simpler: Diagnostic mammography uses individualized additional angles beyond routine screening views. A 90° ML is commonly obtained when triangulation/localization is needed (link-only clinical literature). Detailed ML vs LM selection recipes remain ACR-criteria territory.

lessons.title: XCCL, cleavage, and axillary-tail view names (sourced terms)
lessons.summary: Public terminology sources define XCCL as laterally exaggerated craniocaudal (toward the axilla) and list cleavage and axillary-tail as distinct mammography views. Positioning how-to criteria remain ACR link-only / needs-source.

explanation.heading: XCCL naming
explanation.body: NCI EVS/LOINC synonyms for View XCCL include laterally exaggerated craniocaudal and cranio-caudal view exaggerated to the axilla (also 'internally rotated CC'). The name itself states the tissue goal: lateral/axillary-tail coverage beyond a standard CC.

explanation.heading: Cleavage and axillary tail as named views
explanation.body: NCI EVS lists Cleavage mammography view and Axillary tail mammography view as distinct mammography-view qualifiers. Use the names correctly; do not invent pass/fail positioning checklists here.

explanation.heading: When they appear
explanation.body: These are problem-solving / diagnostic additions when standard CC/MLO do not show the tissue of interest—consistent with NCI's 'more angles' diagnostic framing—not random extra dose.

lessons.example: Standard CC clips the far-lateral tissue that holds a finding: the radiologist requests an XCCL (laterally exaggerated CC) rather than an identical repeat CC.

misconception.belief: XCCL is just another name for MLO.
misconception.correction: XCCL is an exaggerated craniocaudal aimed laterally/toward the axilla, not an MLO.

variants.simpler: Public terminology sources define XCCL as laterally exaggerated craniocaudal (toward the axilla) and list cleavage and axillary-tail as distinct mammography views. Positioning how-to criteria remain ACR link-only / needs-source.

lessons.title: Rolled and tangential views: what public sources actually say
lessons.summary: LOINC/NCI EVS define rolled views as rolling the breast to one side. Link-only clinical literature associates tangential imaging with localizing skin lesions. Full technique cards remain ACR/needs-source.

explanation.heading: Rolled = breast rolled to one side
explanation.body: NCI EVS surfaces LOINC's public change note: 'rolled' means the breast is rolled to one side. That is a purpose-level definition for separating or rearranging overlapping tissue relationships—not a hand-placement cookbook.

explanation.heading: Tangential and skin
explanation.body: Link-only peer-reviewed discussion notes tangential imaging is used to localize skin lesions. Without an accessible public procedure text, Mammo does not invent beam-angle recipes.

explanation.heading: Still a diagnostic tool
explanation.body: Like other additional views, these appear when individualized problem-solving angles are needed (NCI diagnostic framing), not as routine screening defaults.

lessons.example: A radiologist asks for rolled views when two densities overlap on CC and may represent one finding versus two stacked structures.

misconception.belief: Rolled views are the same as implant displacement views.
misconception.correction: Rolled views move native breast tissue relationships; implant displacement is a different technique for implants.

lessons.title: Interventional prep: consent in verification and the time-out
lessons.summary: AHRQ summaries of the Universal Protocol: preprocedure verification (including signed consent), site marking, and a time-out immediately before the invasive procedure—applicable wherever the procedure is performed.

explanation.heading: Three Universal Protocol steps
explanation.body: AHRQ PSNet materials describe preoperative identification/verification, marking the site, and a final time-out just before the procedure.

explanation.heading: Consent lives in verification
explanation.body: Preprocedure verification reviews relevant documents—including the signed consent form—alongside history/physical and related items so discrepancies are caught before starting.

explanation.heading: Time-out is not paperwork theater
explanation.body: The time-out is the last team pause to confirm correct patient, procedure, and site/side before skin entry or needle placement. Facility checklists may add equipment and imaging review; Joint Commission copyrighted text is not copied here.

lessons.example: Before a stereotactic biopsy, the team pauses for a time-out confirming patient identity, left vs right breast, and the planned procedure matching the consent.

misconception.belief: Consent and time-out are only for operating rooms, not breast imaging suites.
misconception.correction: AHRQ notes the time-out applies prior to the procedure regardless of where it is performed.

lessons.title: Triangulation purpose—and where the cookbook is blocked
lessons.summary: Additional 90° lateral views are used in diagnostic pathways to refine lesion location (link-only clinical literature). Step-by-step clock-face triangulation methods from copyrighted teaching atlases are not redistributed; treat those as needs-source until a maintainer performs a link-only check.

explanation.heading: Why triangulation comes up
explanation.body: Findings may project differently on CC and MLO. Diagnostic workups add angles—NCI notes more angles than screening—to estimate where a lesion sits before ultrasound or biopsy.

explanation.heading: ML as a common triangulation view
explanation.body: Link-only literature states a 90° ML view is frequently obtained for diagnostic triangulation. That is purpose-level evidence, not a full method worksheet.

explanation.heading: Blocked detail
explanation.body: Exact paper-ruler / clock-face triangulation procedures taught in commercial radiology texts or ACR positioning manuals remain outside this module. See gap URLs in coverage.json rather than inventing steps.

lessons.example: A mass is lateral on CC and high on MLO; the radiologist adds a true lateral to refine superior-inferior position before scheduling ultrasound.

misconception.belief: Triangulation means drawing triangles on the patient's skin before every screening exam.
misconception.correction: Triangulation here means using multiple mammographic projections to estimate lesion location—not a screening skin-art ritual.

variants.simpler: Additional 90° lateral views are used in diagnostic pathways to refine lesion location (link-only clinical literature).
